instructions: See docs/ratings.md. Give every season a rating on the absolute scale. Rate the player that season, never their career.

seasons.note: Sold to Aston Villa in September 1992 after six starts for Liverpool.
Three league goals in 33 starts for a relegated Forest; the finishing had gone well before the legs.
Veteran squad forward at 35, useful for movement and link play rather than goals.
Nineteen and already a regular in a side that finished third; rated as the promising teenager he was, not the 400-game veteran he became.
A genuinely good shot-stopper carrying a lower-half side; above the Bryan Gunn anchor, well below the elite keepers of the era.
No league goal in seven top-flight seasons; a functional left-back whose value was delivery from wide. Would not be in a modern squad.
Player-manager of a relegated side; still England-standard defensively but stretched by the job and by his age.
Thirty-seven and a squad player, though still an outstanding striker of a dead ball.
No goals in 18 starts; the physical game was still there and nothing else was.
Twenty years old, a double winner and an England starter at Euro 96 within months.
Peak Neville: positionally excellent and an intelligent defender, never an athletic or attacking outlier. Good rather than elite.
Three injury-wrecked seasons at Tottenham followed. The collapse in starts is fitness, but he did genuinely decline as a defender.
The best defender in a Forest side that finished ninth, and comfortable enough on the ball to be unusual for a 1990s centre-half.
PFA Player of the Year; reading and recovery of a genuinely elite defender.
Thirty-six and barely able to train; the reading of the game was intact, the body was not.
Past his peak but still a top-class finisher and the leading scorer.
Three goals in 34 starts at Leeds. Not a barren run for a still-good striker; the finishing itself had gone.
Rated as the twenty-year-old breaking through in the double season, not the player of 1999.
Runner-up for the Ballon d’Or; the best right-sided midfielder in the world that season. Elite delivery and range of passing, ordinary one-v-one.
Joined Blackburn from Coventry in March 1993.
Sixteen goals from wide right in a sixth-placed side and a Scotland regular at the World Cup; his best season.
An attacking wing-back of genuine international quality — a Romania regular across two World Cups — in a role English football barely used.
PFA and FWA Player of the Year in a double season. First touch and vision of an all-time great forward; held below 95 by the absence of pace and the modest goal volume.
Thirty-four and rotated through the Invincibles season; still the best technician in the side.
Banned from late January after Selhurst Park. Rated on the football played, not the games missed.
Captain and champion again but visibly declining; retired at the end of the season aged 30.
Eighteen, six starts, a squad teenager rather than a Premier League footballer yet.
Nine goals in eight starts on arriving from Trabzonspor. A hot streak in a relegation fight, not a step change in ability, so the rating moves three points and not nine.
Twenty and unknown in England; transformed Arsenal’s midfield within weeks of arriving.
Captain of an unbeaten title side. Physically dominant and technically excellent — genuinely world class.
Chronic back and shin problems; effectively his last season of regular football, at 25.
Season ended by a cruciate injury in November.
The aerial focal point of the Quinn/Phillips partnership in a side that finished seventh; his most effective top-flight season, at 32.
Marginalised under Kenny Dalglish and reduced to 20 starts.
PFA and FWA Player of the Year. Elite one-v-one dribbler and crosser; held short of 90 by how little he offered without the ball.
Eleven assists from wide after two seasons out of the side; Wimbledon’s set-piece taker.
